newsitem.title: BELARUS: Clashes as Belarus marchers oppose Russian union.
newsitem.headline: Clashes as Belarus marchers oppose Russian union.

text.p: Baton-wielding police clashed with pro-independence protesters in the capital of Belarus on Wednesday after the small Slav state's president signed an outline Union Treaty with Russia, witnesses said.
Scuffles began when more than 2,000 protesters broke away from a 4,000-strong group of protesters after a peaceful march through Minsk and headed towards the Russian embassy.
Riot police blocked their way and, beating their shields, ran into the crowd when some of the protesters threw stones they had picked up from the street.
The police, some wearing helmets, laid into the crowd with truncheons.
Witnesses said at least 100 people had been detained. Interior Ministry sources told Interfax news agency more than 50 had been detained but many had been released.
An elderly man, who companions said was a professor, fell to the ground unconscious and was taken away in one of at least two ambulances called out to the scene.
Some police were injured by stones. Interfax said two had been taken to hospital.
The protesters were angered by a scaled-down Union Treaty signed in Moscow by Belarus President Alexander Lukashenko and Russian President Boris Yeltsin.
They fear Lukashenko's integration drive could return Belarus to domination by Moscow after five years of independence from the now defunct Soviet Union.
The clashes lasted about an hour. Several reporters were detained and Irina Khalip, who works for a local opposition paper and Russia's weekly Itogi analytical magazine, was among those beaten.
Svetlana Stasun, 55, stood weeping on the pavement when the street emptied, saying she had tried to stop special OMON forces dragging a teenage protester off by the hair.
"I cannot watch them beating these kids. I tried to help a young boy, but the OMON threatened to beat me too," she said.
"I'm not a politician but as far as I understand Moscow has not given up power to Lukashenko, but he has given up Belarus".
Yeltsin said after he signed the document that each side maintained its sovereignty. The deal was also a far cry from one which Lukashenko had backed but was opposed by Russian liberals.
That version would have put him closer to his dream of eventually uniting his former Soviet republic of 10 million people with Russia, which has almost 150 million people.
Street protests have become a regular event in Minsk, especially since Lukashenko won a controversial referendum last November which vastly increased his powers.
But most Belarussians, especially outside Minsk, believe he will keep order and share his nostalgia for the Soviet past.

An earlier rally by several hundred communists waving portraits of the moustachioed Lukashenko and banners reading "NATO off Belarus' borders" and "Hands off the Belarussian people and its president" passed without major incident.
Nationalists gathered on a bridge above the rally, whistling and jeering and shouting "Shame! Shame!", but the opposing factions did not fight each other.
